The word \textit{prairie} is a keyword for the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card. (This omission was corrected in print by December 2019.)
``Turkey'' does not count as a geography term for the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card, and neither does ``turkey vulture'' (turkey vultures are named after the bird, not the country).
``Wood'' (singular) in a bird's name is not a geography term for the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card, so birds such as \textbf{Wood Stork} and woodswallows do not count.
\textbf{Red Junglefowl} counts toward the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card, since ``jungle'' appears in its name.

The only keywords that qualify a bird to count toward this bonus card are those listed thereon, including \textit{prairie} (which is printed on this bonus card only in newer printings), and those in the relevant sections of the expansion rulebooks.
\textbf{Cartographer} awards a flat bonus for the tier reached, not points per qualifying bird: at least 2 qualifying birds scores 3 points, at least 4 scores 7 points.
On this bonus card ``name'' refers only to the common name, not the scientific name.
This bird counts toward the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card. (In early printings that bonus card did list include the keyword \textit{prairie}.)
The 3-point bonus applies when there are 4--5 qualifying birds on your player mat, not 2--3. (This misprint was corrected in the third printing, and a corrected card is available in the update pack.)

\textbf{Baya Weaver} does not count toward the \textbf{Photographer} bonus card. That card looks for colors as words or as part of compound words, and ``Baya'' is its own word, not a compound of ``bay'' and ``a''.
\textit{Rainbow} is not a color and does not count toward this bonus card.
\textit{Redstart} and \textit{yellowthroat} both count toward this bonus card; a full list of qualifying colors appears on page 4 of the Appendix.

The only keywords that qualify a bird to count toward this bonus card are those listed thereon, those in the relevant sections of the expansion rulebooks (excluding \textit{honey} in the \textit{European Expansion} rulebook---see \textbf{Honey}), and \textit{violet}. (\textit{Violet} currently occurs only on the \textbf{Violet-Green Swallow}, which already contains another keyword for this bonus card.) Substrings of bird names that coincide with color names do not count toward this bonus when not referring to colors (e.g., the \textit{red} in \textbf{Barred Owl}), but see \textbf{Northern Bobwhite}.
The point values on this bonus card are totals, not per-bird: if you have the number of qualifying birds shown, you gain that number of points in total.

This bird is worth 5 points, not 4. (This misprint was corrected in the third printing, and a corrected card is available in the update pack.)

\textbf{Hooded Merganser} activates another bird's brown power, and it may activate a bird's power regardless of whether that bird is to the left or right of it.
\textbf{Hooded Merganser}'s power is activated as a brown power, so it can only repeat another brown power -- specifically a [predator] power -- and the repeated bird must be in the same habitat.

When \textbf{Pileated Woodpecker}'s power is activated, other players may choose not to lay an [egg].

``May'' indicates a binary option: you may do exactly as instructed, or you may not do it at all. It never licenses substituting a different action. When paying a bird's food cost, you may exchange any 2 food tokens to stand in for 1 food of any type you lack. This exchange may be used multiple times in the same payment (e.g., paying 4 [seed] to replace 2 missing foods). The 2-for-1 exchange is only available when playing a bird.

If you perform more than one action ``at the end of your turn'', you may perform those actions in any order.

This bird counts double toward precisely the end-of-round bonuses that count birds, not those that count other quantities. When in your hand this card does not count toward end-of-round bonuses.

If a pink power is triggered by another bird's power, the pink power is resolved after the other bird's power has been resolved.

The two clauses of \textbf{Galah}'s power are independent; the order is simply order of operations. Even if the chosen player does not find a [seed] in the birdfeeder, you still tuck 2 [card] from the deck behind this bird.
If another player activates \textbf{Laughing Kookaburra}'s [predator] power and it succeeds (they gain a food), \textbf{Black-Billed Magpie}'s power triggers and you gain 1 [die] from the birdfeeder.
\textbf{Black-Billed Magpie} is not a predator bird and does not count for the \textbf{Falconer} bonus card; a bird is a predator only if it has the [predator] icon before its power text.

\textbf{Laughing Kookaburra} has a [predator] power. If another player activates it and it succeeds (they gain a food), \textbf{Black-Billed Magpie}'s power triggers and you gain 1 [die] from the birdfeeder.

The [wild] symbol always includes [nectar], so \textbf{Chihuahuan Raven} may take [nectar] from the supply with its power. The Oceania rulebook suggests that players who find this too powerful remove \textbf{Chihuahuan Raven} and \textbf{Common Raven} from the deck when playing with the Oceania Expansion.
The [wild] (``any food'') symbol includes [nectar] among the foods you may choose, but you are never obligated to choose [nectar].
[nectar] is wild for paying bird costs and may be spent in place of any specific food, but a [nectar] icon in a cost must be paid with [nectar]; only a [wild] icon accepts any food.

\textbf{Spangled Drongo} only triggers between your turns, never on your own turn. If you activate \textbf{Eastern Rosella} on your turn, causing all players to gain 1 [nectar], \textbf{Spangled Drongo} does not activate.

When another player uses \textbf{Green Heron}'s power to trade a food token for [nectar], that counts as gaining [nectar], so \textbf{Spangled Drongo} triggers - it is not a net gain of food, but it is still a gain.

Receiving [nectar] as a gift counts as gaining [nectar], so when a player uses \textbf{Red-Winged Parrot} to give [nectar] to another player, the receiving player has gained [nectar] and \textbf{Spangled Drongo} may be activated.
\textbf{Spangled Drongo} triggers when another player gains [nectar] from the supply by discarding [fruit] with \textbf{Mistletoebird}'s power.

\textbf{Spangled Drongo} triggers whenever another player gains [nectar] by any means, not only with the ``gain food'' action - for example, if another player gains 1 [nectar] from the supply through a bird power. As a ``once between turns'' power, it can trigger only once between each of your turns.
Deciding how many additional bonus cards to draw, and discarding the corresponding [wild], is a one-time decision, so you cannot discard food one at a time.
You look at the first bonus card drawn with \textbf{Kea}'s power before deciding how many additional bonus cards to draw.
You keep only 1 bonus card out of all those drawn with this power, including the first one drawn before discarding [wild].

A bonus card with tiered scoring awards only the amount for the tier reached, not points per qualifying bird. On \textbf{Cartographer} you must have at least 2 qualifying birds to score 3 points and at least 4 to score 7 points.
Only one scoring category on a bonus card is scored: score either for 1 set of the 4 nest types or for 2 or more sets, not both.
The [rodent] discarded for \textbf{Korimako}'s power cannot be cached food; cached food may only be spent when a card specifically refers to it, and otherwise is only worth points.
The [rodent] come from your own personal supply, not from the birdfeeder; throughout the rulebook, ``discard'' refers to paying food from your supply.
This bird's power allows resetting or refilling the tray only once; you may not keep resetting until a [cavity] or [star] nest bird appears.

\textbf{Forster's Tern}'s ``Draw 1 [card]'' does not specify a source, so you may take either a face-up card from the tray or the top card of the deck. (Contrast \textbf{Great Horned Owl}, whose ``Look at a [card] from the deck'' must use the top card of the deck.)

The card drawn with \textbf{Forster's Tern} goes into your hand; \textbf{Great Crested Grebe} and \textbf{Wilson's Storm Petrel} work differently, keeping their drawn cards separate from your hand until the end of your turn, when you keep 1 and discard the rest.

\textbf{Forster's Tern} requires discarding from your hand, so if your hand is empty at the end of your turn (for instance because you tucked all your cards with \textbf{Common Chiffchaff}), you discard nothing.

You do not need to keep a card in hand to satisfy \textbf{Wood Duck}'s power. If you draw 2 [card] with \textbf{Wood Duck} and then play or tuck all the cards in your hand (for example with \textbf{Common Chiffchaff}), having no card to discard at the end of your turn is legal.
Tucking all your cards with \textbf{Common Chiffchaff} can leave your hand empty, in which case \textbf{Forster's Tern}'s end-of-turn discard discards nothing.
[nectar] counts as a food type for this bird's power, so you may choose [nectar] and all players gain 1 [nectar] from the supply.
A [wild] food cost symbol does not count as an [invertebrate] or a [rodent] for \textbf{Brown Falcon}: a card whose food cost includes only [wild] is discarded rather than tucked.

For end-of-round goals that name two food types in the food cost of your birds, count every icon of either type printed in the food costs of your played birds; a single bird does not need to require both. For example, with 5 [fruit] icons and 8 [seed] icons among your played birds, your number for the goal is 13.

For end-of-round goals that name two food types in the food cost of your birds, count every icon of either type printed in the food costs of your played birds; a single bird does not need to require both. For example, with 5 [fruit] icons and 8 [seed] icons among your played birds, your number for the goal is 13.

You do not need to keep a card in hand to discard: if you draw 2 [card] with \textbf{Wood Duck} and then play or tuck your whole hand (for example with \textbf{Common Chiffchaff}), having nothing to discard at the end of your turn is legal.

For end-of-round goals that name two food types in the food cost of your birds, count every icon of either type printed in the food costs of your played birds; a single bird does not need to require both. For example, with 5 [fruit] icons and 8 [seed] icons among your played birds, your number for the goal is 13.
When counting birds in your [grassland] for this bird's power, include \textbf{Plains-Wanderer} itself. If it were excluded, the power would say ``each other bird''.

With no open space in the habitat for the bird, you cannot use \textbf{Gould's Finch}'s power at all: if you can't play the bird, you don't get to use its ``when played'' or ``game end'' power either.

When a bird is played using a ``game end'' (yellow) power such as \textbf{Dovekie} or \textbf{Yellow-Eyed Penguin}, you still gain the benefits of its ``when played'' (white) and ``game end'' (yellow) powers, even if the yellow power does not say so. \textbf{Gould's Finch} states this explicitly only for extra clarity.

Nectar in your personal supply is returned to the supply during step 2 of the end of round 6, before ``game end'' powers such as \textbf{Grey-Headed Mannikin}'s are activated, so that nectar is no longer available to help pay the food cost of the bird played with this power.

With no open space in the habitat for the bird, you cannot use \textbf{Grey-Headed Mannikin}'s power at all: if you can't play the bird, you don't get to use its ``when played'' or ``game end'' power either.

When a bird is played using a ``game end'' (yellow) power such as \textbf{Dovekie} or \textbf{Yellow-Eyed Penguin}, you still gain the benefits of its ``when played'' (white) and ``game end'' (yellow) powers, even if the yellow power does not say so. \textbf{Grey-Headed Mannikin} states this explicitly only for extra clarity.
The player you give the [rodent] to must accept it; they cannot decline in order to prevent you from laying eggs.
All 3 [egg] are laid at once as part of resolving the power, essentially ``lay 3 [egg] on this bird if you can''; eggs already on the bird may limit its remaining egg capacity.
The condition ``If its wingspan is over 65cm'' is correct and not a misprint; unlike other predators, this bird tucks the drawn [card] when the wingspan is large.

End-of-round goals are scored before end-of-game powers are activated (steps 4 and 6 of the ``End of Round Reference'' tile included with the \textit{Oceania Expansion}). Score the end-of-round goal first, then activate \textbf{Australian Magpie}, so discarding [egg] with its power cannot change your score for an egg-based goal.

Powers that say ``Roll all dice not in birdfeeder'' are always resolved outside of the birdfeeder: do not roll those dice back into the birdfeeder. Only the dice rolled outside the birdfeeder are considered, not the dice sitting in the birdfeeder. If there are no dice outside the birdfeeder, this power has no dice to roll and gains nothing. Also, a ``When Played'' power resolves only after the bird has been played, so its cost must be paid first---you cannot use \textbf{Brown Pelican}'s power to gain the [fish] needed to pay for it. When a power refers to the ``player(s) with the fewest'' something, the ``(s)'' means that if several players are tied for the fewest, they all gain the benefit. Eggs must always be placed on a nest with available space; you may not hold eggs to the side of your player mat.

Powers that say ``Roll all dice not in birdfeeder'' are always resolved outside of the birdfeeder: do not roll those dice back into the birdfeeder. Only the dice rolled outside the birdfeeder are considered, not the dice sitting in the birdfeeder. If there are no dice outside the birdfeeder, this power has no dice to roll and gains nothing. Also, a ``When Played'' power resolves only after the bird has been played, so its cost must be paid first---you cannot use \textbf{Brown Pelican}'s power to gain the [fish] needed to pay for it. When a power refers to the ``player(s) with the fewest'' something, the ``(s)'' means that if several players are tied for the fewest, they all gain the benefit. Eggs must always be placed on a nest with available space; you may not hold eggs to the side of your player mat.

These powers are literal and the ``may'' is a genuine choice: food you gain goes to your supply, and you may instead choose to cache any or all of it on this bird, where it scores 1 point at the end of the game instead of being available to spend.
The gained [seed] goes to your personal supply unless you choose to cache it on this bird; caching is optional.
A bird with a [star] (wild) nest counts as having a [cavity] nest for \textbf{Blyth's Hornbill}, so you may discard all [egg] from a bird with a [star] nest.
\textbf{Budgerigar} is a brown ``when activated'' bird; the Oceania appendix listing it as ``when played'' is an error.
A [star] wingspan bird may be treated as any wingspan you choose at the moment it matters, so you may decide whether a [star] bird in the tray counts as the smallest bird.

You are always limited by the [egg] limit of each bird, including when laying [egg] with an end-of-round or game-end power; if the birds in your [wetland] are already at their [egg] limit, no [egg] can be laid.

A [predator] power ``succeeds'' when its element of chance produces the result it is looking for (for example, looking at the top card of the deck and finding a bird with a small enough wingspan to tuck). \textbf{Black Vulture}'s power triggers whenever another player's [predator] finds what it is looking for.
Activate this power immediately when another player's [predator] succeeds, not at the end of that player's turn.
You must discard an actual [fish] to activate \textbf{American White Pelican}; food substitutions only apply when playing a bird, not when paying a cost in a bird's power.
Zero birds counts as the fewest birds, so a player with no birds in their [wetland] can be the player with the fewest birds and draw 1 [card].

As you draw face-up cards, they are not immediately refilled. Instead, wait until the end of your turn before refilling empty spaces on the bird tray. \textbf{Royal Spoonbill} allows you to reset (discard all cards on the tray and refill it) or refill the tray before drawing.

The bird card display is refilled at the end of each player's turn, including the final turn of a round, so it is refilled after a turn using \textbf{Australian Ibis}. The round-end steps then completely refresh the card row.
Discarded bird cards and bonus cards are discarded face up, including the card discarded when using \textbf{Australian Ibis}'s power.

When activating \textbf{Parrot Crossbill}, if all dice in the birdfeeder show the same face you may first refill the birdfeeder by rolling all dice, even though the [seed] is gained from the supply rather than from the die you remove.
A bonus card discarded to score \textbf{Red-Crowned Crane} goes to the discarded bonus card pile and may be retrieved later with \textbf{Wrybill}, allowing the same bonus card to be scored twice.

A bonus card discarded via \textbf{Red-Crowned Crane} cannot be scored at game end, so \textbf{Great Indian Bustard}'s instruction to ``also score it normally at game end'' no longer applies to that bonus card.

\textbf{Great Indian Bustard}'s ``Also score it normally at game end'' only clarifies that scoring the bonus card immediately does not prevent scoring it again at game end; you score it at game end only if you still have that bonus card. If you later discard that same bonus card (for example with \textbf{Red-Crowned Crane}), you do not score it at game end.

When scoring a bonus card immediately with \textbf{Red-Crowned Crane}, ignore any ``at game end'' wording on the bonus card and score it based on the current game state. For \textbf{Winter Feeder}, score based on the food currently in your personal supply.

For \textbf{Behaviorist}, a column is a straight stack of card slots within a single row position across the three habitats. The birds with 3 different power colors must all be in the same column; colors matched diagonally or in other arrangements do not count.
When using \textbf{Masked Lapwing}'s power, a die showing two food types (such as a [nectar] face) counts as both types: gain 1 of each type shown, up to a maximum of 1 of each type overall.

\textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} does not count for bonus cards that reward birds letting you score or draw bonus cards (such as \textbf{Endangered Species Protector}), even if the power it copied did so. Only the abilities printed on the card matter during bonus scoring.

Resolve the copied ``When Played'' power as if its text replaced \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet}'s own: it applies to your board, not your neighbor's. Copying \textbf{Great Indian Bustard} therefore scores one of your own bonus cards, caching [seed] on \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet}.

\textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} copies only the ``When Played'' power, not the copied bird's food cost, and the power only does what it can do for the copying bird: copying \textbf{Eastern Imperial Eagle} or \textbf{Bonelli's Eagle} does nothing, because \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} has no [rodent] in its own cost.

The copied power lasts for that turn only; at the end of the turn \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} no longer has it, so a copied bonus-card power does not make it count toward the \textbf{Endangered Species} bonus card at game end. Copying \textbf{Bonelli's Eagle} or \textbf{Eastern Imperial Eagle} does nothing, since those powers refer to [rodent] in the bird's cost and \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} costs no [rodent].
A ``neighbor'' in Wingspan is the players to your immediate left and right, not all players at the table.
The [wild] (``any food'') symbol always includes [nectar], so you may cache [nectar] with this bird's power if you still have [nectar] in your supply when the round-end power activates.
For powers that roll ``any'' dice you may roll dice from inside the birdfeeder, outside it, or a mix; dice taken from the birdfeeder stay out of it after rolling, until the birdfeeder is refilled.
If there is no [fish] cached on \textbf{Great Cormorant}, ignore the first clause and go straight to rolling 2 [die]; move 1 [fish] to your supply only when one is cached there.
Tied scores do not count as ascending or descending—5 is not higher than 5—so a run of birds worth 5, 5, 3, 3, 3 points does not form an ascending or descending sequence.

The Ranger bonus cards use strict ascending/descending, so repeated point values break the series (unlike \textbf{Data Analyst}, which explicitly allows equal wingspans). With scores of 6, 5, 5, 4, 3 in [forest], \textbf{Forest Ranger} scores only the longest strictly ascending or descending series: 5, 4, 3.

Tied scores do not count as ascending or descending - 5 is not higher than 5 - so scores of 1-2-2-3-5 in [forest] count as a sequence of three, not five, and a run of 5, 5, 3, 3, 3 forms no sequence at all.
Tied scores do not count as ascending or descending—5 is not higher than 5—so a run of birds worth 5, 5, 3, 3, 3 points does not form an ascending or descending sequence.
The second sentence of \textbf{Sri Lanka Frogmouth}'s power is not dependent on the first: all players may discard 1 [card] to gain 1 [invertebrate] regardless of whether the die roll succeeded.
Zero counts as ``fewest'': player(s) with no birds in their [forest] gain 1 [die] from the birdfeeder.

You may decline to activate \textbf{Hermit Thrush}, but if you do activate it, the player(s) with the fewest birds in their [forest] gain their [die] - activating a power is optional, but the whole power then resolves.
When a power tells you to roll ``any'' dice, you choose where those dice come from (birdfeeder or table). The dice you roll are placed on the table.

Any player may decline a benefit, whether it comes from their own power or from another player's power. With \textbf{Brolga}, the chosen player may decline to lay the [egg], and you still draw 2 [card] either way. Having food stolen is not a benefit, so a player being stolen from has no choice.

Unless a power specifies that cards must be drawn from the deck or from the bird tray, you may choose where to draw each [card] from: the face-up cards in the bird tray or the top of the deck. On \textbf{Indian Peafowl}, the additional [card] you draw may come from either source, even though the first 2 [card] must come from the deck.

The other players keep the [card] they drew only if that card has a [invertebrate] or [seed] in its food cost; it is not the card you drew that determines this. Despite the different wording, the power works the same way as \textbf{Little Egret}.
The other players must reveal the [card] they draw, to prove whether it has a [invertebrate] or [seed] in its food cost.

With \textbf{Plumbeous Redstart}, the other players keep the [card] they drew only if that card has a [invertebrate] or [seed] in its food cost; it is not the card you drew that determines this. Despite the different wording, the power works the same way as \textbf{Little Egret}.

If \textbf{Spoon-Billed Sandpiper} is played at game end (for instance via a yellow power that lets you play a bird then), its power is still followed in full, including the portion letting other players discard any 2 resources to draw 2 new bonus cards and keep 1.
The 2 resources other players discard must come from their personal supply; cached food on birds may not be discarded for this.

Dice chosen for this power are rolled outside the birdfeeder. If choosing them empties the birdfeeder, all 5 [die] are rerolled into the birdfeeder (resetting it) once the rolling is complete, before play continues.
Where a power says to roll ``any'' dice, you may choose whether the dice come from the birdfeeder or from outside it. Either way, dice rolled for a bird power stay out of the birdfeeder.
Because caching is optional, you may instead add the [seed] gained with \textbf{Red-Bellied Woodpecker}'s power to your personal food supply.
[seed] cached on \textbf{Coal Tit} or \textbf{Eurasian Nuthatch} is not in your supply, so it does not count toward \textbf{Winter Feeder} even though you may spend it at any time.
When scoring this bonus card immediately with \textbf{Red-Crowned Crane}, ignore the ``at game end'' wording and score based on the food currently in your personal supply.
\textbf{Great Indian Bustard} can score bonus cards that specify ``at end of game'' or ``at game end,'' such as \textbf{Visionary Leader} and \textbf{Winter Feeder}, when its power is used mid-game.

A duet token placed in the reset box of the Asia goal mat cannot be removed to reset the bird tray or the birdfeeder on the same turn it was placed; only on a later turn. Duet tokens are placed between steps 5 and 6 of your turn, so a bird that lets you play an additional bird (e.g. \textbf{Small Minivet}) does not allow you to spend a token placed earlier in that same turn.
Only the food types named on \textbf{Small Minivet} itself may be ignored in the cost of the additional bird - the printed text takes precedence over the general wording in the appendix.

The text printed on \textbf{Small Minivet} and \textbf{Trumpeter Finch} takes precedence over the general wording in the appendix: only the food types named on the bird itself may be ignored in the cost of the additional bird.
This bird's power may be used to lay an [egg] on a bird with an egg limit of 0, since it allows going 2 over the egg limit.
Where a power says to roll ``any'' dice, you may choose whether the dice come from the birdfeeder or from outside it. Either way, dice rolled for a bird power stay out of the birdfeeder.
\textbf{Desert Wheatear} counts toward the \textbf{Anatomist} bonus card (``ear'').

``Also score it normally at game end'' only clarifies that scoring the bonus card now does not prevent scoring it again at game end; you score it at game end only if you still hold that bonus card. Discard it later (for example with \textbf{Red-Crowned Crane}) and you score nothing at game end.

When \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} copies a neighbor's ``When Played'' power, resolve it as if the copied text replaced \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet}'s own text: it applies to your board, not your neighbor's. Copying \textbf{Great Indian Bustard} therefore scores one of your own bonus cards, caching [seed] on \textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet}.
\textbf{Great Indian Bustard} can score bonus cards that specify ``at end of game'' or ``at game end,'' such as \textbf{Visionary Leader} and \textbf{Winter Feeder}, when its power is used mid-game.

Cache [seed] equal to the bonus card's value when the Bustard is played (each cached [seed] is worth 1 point), then score the same bonus card again at game end for its condition at that time. Example: \textbf{Visionary Leader} with 6 [card] in hand caches 4 [seed]; at game end score \textbf{Visionary Leader} for the [card] then in hand.
\textbf{Great Indian Bustard} can score bonus cards that specify ``at end of game'' or ``at game end,'' such as \textbf{Visionary Leader} and \textbf{Winter Feeder}, when its power is used mid-game.

Birds in hand that score for \textbf{Visionary Leader} do not count for \textbf{Endangered Species}, which counts only birds played on your player mat; cards referring to bird cards look only at played birds unless stated otherwise.

\textbf{Great Indian Bustard} caches [seed] equal to \textbf{Visionary Leader}'s value when the Bustard is played (each [seed] is worth 1 point), and \textbf{Visionary Leader} is also scored normally at game end. Example: 6 [card] in hand when the Bustard is played caches 4 [seed]; at game end score for the [card] then in hand.

You must end the turn with at least 1 of the [card] drawn with \textbf{Wilson's Storm Petrel}, but the others may be disposed of in other ways during the turn (for example, tucked with \textbf{Common Grackle}) instead of being discarded.
Keep the [card] drawn with \textbf{Wilson's Storm Petrel} separate from your hand until the end of your turn, when you keep 1 of them and discard the rest.

Eggs laid by \textbf{Common Tailorbird}'s end-of-game power do not count toward the round 4 end-of-round goal, because that goal is scored before game-end powers are activated. See the reference tile for the order of operations.

For \textbf{Common Tailorbird}, ``contiguous'' means orthogonally adjacent: directly to the left, right, above, or below, never diagonal. The group may zig-zag across rows and columns as long as each bird in the group is orthogonally adjacent to at least one other bird in the group.

Duet tokens are only placed when you play a bird, so no one places a duet token when \textbf{Blue Rock-Thrush} or \textbf{Spotted Dove} moves to another player's mat. If a bird is later played on that space, a duet token is placed as normal.
When \textbf{Spotted Dove} moves to another player's mat, any cached food, [egg], or tucked [card] on it are discarded (Wingspan Asia appendix, p. 9).

No duet token is placed when \textbf{Spotted Dove} moves to another player's mat, since duet tokens are only placed when you play a bird. If a bird is later played on that space, a duet token is placed as normal.
When \textbf{Large-Billed Crow} caches [nectar], place it on the bird, not in your personal supply of spent [nectar].

\textbf{Baya Weaver} does not count toward the \textbf{Photographer} bonus card. That card looks for colors as words or as part of compound words, and ``Baya'' is its own word, not a compound of ``bay'' and ``a''.
\textbf{Spangled Drongo}'s power triggers when another player gains [nectar] in any way, including gaining [nectar] from the supply by discarding [fruit] with \textbf{Mistletoebird}'s power.
Powers that refer to types of birds (e.g., \textbf{Carrion Crow}, which caches 1 [rodent] for each [predator] a player has) always refer to birds played on a player mat, never to birds in hand.
\textbf{Willie-Wagtail}: you may reset the card tray only once per activation of this power. If no [card] with a [bowl] or [star] nest is available after that reset, you gain no card.
\textbf{Blue-Winged Warbler} may be played in either the [forest] or the [grassland].
For bonus cards that count birds with a color in their name, the color may be part of a larger word: \textbf{Silvereye} counts as a bird with a color in its name.
``Wood'' (singular) in a bird's name is not a geography term for the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card, so birds such as \textbf{Wood Stork} and woodswallows do not count.
The 2 [wild] gained with \textbf{Gray Wagtail}'s round-end power may be taken as [nectar], but round-end powers resolve before unused [nectar] is discarded, so that [nectar] is immediately lost.

The food cached by \textbf{Willow Tit} comes from the birdfeeder, so the corresponding die must be removed from the birdfeeder. If the birdfeeder contains no [invertebrate], [seed], or [fruit], nothing is cached.
Your neighbors are only the players directly to your right and left — at most 2 players, regardless of the number of players in the game.

With \textbf{Forster's Tern} you are not required to keep a card in hand for the end-of-turn discard; if you have tucked or otherwise used all of your cards, there is nothing to discard. \textbf{Great Crested Grebe} and \textbf{Wilson's Storm Petrel} work differently: keep the cards drawn with those powers separate from your hand until the end of your turn, when you keep 1 of them and discard the rest.
\textbf{Red Junglefowl} counts toward the \textbf{Cartographer} bonus card, since ``jungle'' appears in its name.
With \textbf{European Turtle Dove}, first draw 1 new bonus card, then choose exactly one of the three benefits: gain 1 [die] from the birdfeeder, lay 1 [egg] on any bird, or draw 1 [card].
\textbf{Red-Tailed Hawk} draws from the top of the deck, not from the 3 face-up cards on the bird tray, so its power can always be activated — there will always be cards in the deck.

You must score all of your bonus cards at the end of the game (even if you earn 0 [star] from them), so you cannot decline to score a bonus card because an opponent copied it with \textbf{Greater Adjutant} or \textbf{Indian Vulture} and would score more from it than you.
When the order of Game End powers matters, activate them in clockwise order starting with the player who has the first-player token.

You must score all of your bonus cards at the end of the game (even if you earn 0 [star] from them), so you cannot decline to score a bonus card because an opponent copied it with \textbf{Greater Adjutant} or \textbf{Indian Vulture} and would score more from it than you.
When the order of Game End powers matters, activate them in clockwise order starting with the player who has the first-player token.

\textbf{Common Myna}'s habitat restriction applies only to where it can be played, not to where it can move. If it copies a power that moves a bird to another habitat, such as \textbf{Blue Grosbeak}'s, \textbf{Common Myna} may move out of the [grassland].

Copying a power places the other bird's power on \textbf{Common Myna} on your own player mat. If you copy a power that itself copies ``a power of a bird in the [grassland] of the player on your left'', you must still copy from another player's [grassland], not your own.

\textbf{Food Web Expert} counts only birds whose food cost is [invertebrate] and nothing else. A bird with any other food symbol in its cost, even as an alternative, counts for 0. The appendix reads: ``Count the number of birds that have [invertebrate] in their food cost and no other symbols.''

When gaining food from the birdfeeder with \textbf{Hawfinch} or \textbf{European Honey Buzzard} after resetting it, dice showing the [invertebrate]/[seed] face count: \textbf{Hawfinch} may take the [seed] from such a die, and \textbf{European Honey Buzzard} gains the [invertebrate] from such a die along with all other [invertebrate] showing.
[nectar] may be discarded to pay the [wild] cost of \textbf{Crimson Chat}. The discarded [nectar] goes to the spent nectar area of your player mat.
[nectar] may be cached with \textbf{House Crow}. Cached [nectar] is placed on the bird, not in the spent nectar area of your player mat.
If you choose to use \textbf{North Island Brown Kiwi}'s power, you must follow all of its instructions; you cannot skip discarding a bonus card and still draw bonus cards.
You may not reset the birdfeeder before using \textbf{Western Screech-Owl}'s power, even if it contains only one food type, because you are not gaining food from the birdfeeder.
\textbf{European Serin}'s power requires discarding all food tokens from your personal supply, not just all of one food type. You must have at least 1 food to activate it.
When using \textbf{Tufted Puffin}, roll the same set of dice all three times; dice that roll [fish] are not removed from the pool between rolls.

``Resetting the birdfeeder'' means rerolling all the dice in the birdfeeder, however it comes about, so \textbf{Laughing Gull} also triggers (once between turns) on a reroll caused by all remaining dice showing the same face or only one die being left.

\textbf{Laughing Gull} triggers on any birdfeeder reset during another player's turn, regardless of cause -- e.g. if their ``gain food'' action empties the birdfeeder because you took the last die with \textbf{Australian Owlet-Nightjar}, that reset still activates it.

\textbf{Laughing Gull}'s power triggers whenever the birdfeeder is reset during another player's turn, regardless of which effect caused the reset. For example, if another player's ``gain food'' action empties the birdfeeder because you took the last die with \textbf{Australian Owlet-Nightjar}, the birdfeeder reset on their turn still activates \textbf{Laughing Gull}.

A bird played for free with \textbf{Yellow-Eyed Penguin} still triggers its ``when played'' power, but powers that refer to a paid cost have no effect: \textbf{Bonelli's Eagle} tucks no [card] when played for free.

A bird played using a ``game end'' (yellow) power such as \textbf{Yellow-Eyed Penguin} still gives you its ``when played'' (white) and ``game end'' (yellow) powers, even if the yellow power does not say so; \textbf{Gould's Finch} and \textbf{Grey-Headed Mannikin} state this only for extra clarity.
Food cached on \textbf{Ivory Gull} may only be spent on the cost of a bird power, never to play a bird -- including a bird played via another bird's power, such as \textbf{Tufted Titmouse}.
Food cached on \textbf{Ivory Gull} may be spent just like food in your personal supply whenever a bird power asks you to pay food to do something.

\textbf{Great Kiskadee} and \textbf{Tropical Kingbird}: After moving with the action cube, continue activating birds only in the new habitat -- you do not activate the core action of the new habitat. For pink ``once between turns'' powers that trigger on another player taking a specific core action, the action taken is the one where the cube started, since the core action happens at the beginning of the turn.

\textbf{Rose-Ringed Parakeet} does not count toward the \textbf{Endangered Species Protector} bonus card even if it was used to copy a ``When Played'' power that scored or drew bonus cards. Only the abilities printed on the card matter during bonus scoring.
When this bird's power attracts a hummingbird, you activate that hummingbird card's benefit.
\textbf{Great Eared Nightjar}'s power looks for the [forest] icon printed on the drawn bird cards. Any bird with a [forest] icon counts, even if it also has other habitat icons.

When \textbf{Blue-and-Yellow Macaw} attracts a hummingbird, it may be placed in any hummingbird slot, not only one in the [forest]. Card abilities that attract or return hummingbirds are not limited to the habitat the bird is in.

The eggs placed by \textbf{Rufous Hornero} are placeholders: they do not count as eggs in your preserve for any other purpose, so they do not count toward end-of-round goals or end-of-game scoring. Those spaces are still empty for powers that count empty spaces.

An [egg] placed by this power can only help pay the egg cost of the bird played on top of it; it cannot be spent on a bird in another habitat or slot. If that bird needs no eggs (column 1), discard the egg.

This power only attracts hummingbirds; it does not let you return hummingbirds already on your player mat. You may attract only as many as you have open hummingbird spaces (1 or 2), and if all your hummingbird spaces are full you attract none. Nectar shown on an attracted hummingbird is gained as normal, even though this is a round end power.
Standard tucking rules apply to the hummingbird tucked behind this bird.
\textbf{Southern Lapwing}'s power is an independent choice ([egg] or [card]) for each empty slot in your [forest], so you may mix the two: with 5 empty slots you could lay 3 [egg] and draw 2 [card].

\textbf{California Scrub-Jay}: ``Upgrading an action'' refers to the optional portion of the core action benefits printed on the player mat. Any time another player pays for and uses such an upgraded benefit -- including the choice between multiple upgrade options in a habitat, such as rerolling the birdfeeder or gaining an extra food -- it counts for this bird.

When using \textbf{Titicaca Grebe}'s power, the drawn bonus cards are looked at, not chosen blindly: you look at them and choose 1, then the next player looks at the remaining cards and chooses 1, and so on.
If the card drawn with \textbf{Blue-Headed Parrot}'s power has both [seed] and [fruit] in its food cost, you still gain only 1 food token from the supply; choose which one.

For powers that check which action types you used this round, such as \textbf{White Wagtail}, look at where each action cube ended up, as that is the game's way of remembering. A bird such as \textbf{Lineated Woodpecker} that moves with the action cube to another habitat therefore changes which action the cube records.

After \textbf{Lineated Woodpecker} moves with the action cube and you continue your turn in the new habitat, you activate only the brown powers in the habitat where the cube now is; you do not activate the remaining powers of the habitat it left.

With \textbf{Garden Warbler}, the additional bird is played first and completely, including its own ``when played'' power, and only then is 1 [egg] laid on both birds. If the additional bird is \textbf{Red Kite} (or a similar bird) played on top of \textbf{Garden Warbler}, turning \textbf{Garden Warbler} into a tucked card, the egg laying still takes place.

These powers are literal and the ``may'' is a genuine choice: food you gain goes to your supply, and you may instead choose to cache any or all of it on this bird, where it scores 1 point at the end of the game instead of being available to spend.
\textbf{Canada Jay}: you may cache 1 [wild] from your personal supply and then immediately gain 1 food of that same type from the general supply in the same activation.

Hummingbird bonuses are only triggered when a hummingbird marker moves up the track, so moving a marker down with \textbf{Crested Oropendola} does not trigger the bonus of the space it lands on. To trigger a bonus again you must move down twice and then up at least once; an infinite loop is not possible.
For \textbf{Orinoco Goose}, adjacent [star] nest birds count as [cavity] birds.

When a bird is played using a ``game end'' (yellow) power such as \textbf{Dovekie} or \textbf{Yellow-Eyed Penguin}, you still gain the benefits of its ``when played'' (white) and ``game end'' (yellow) powers, even if the yellow power does not say so. \textbf{Gould's Finch} and \textbf{Grey-Headed Mannikin} state this explicitly only for extra clarity.

\textbf{Red-Legged Seriema}'s power looks at the birdfeeder after a single reset, checking simultaneously for [seed] and [rodent]. You may not claim some of those tokens and then reset the birdfeeder again to gain more.
Score 1 point for each [hummingbird] space on your hummingbird track that you have reached or exceeded.
``May'' creates a choice. On \textbf{Red-Headed Woodpecker}, you may decline to cache the [seed] and instead keep it as a normal food resource to spend later.
